hypothesis: Weather foundation models such as Aurora and GraphCast, which autoregressively generate multi-day global weather trajectories at high spatial resolution, can be directly repurposed as probabilistic scenario engines for long-horizon renewable energy planning by coupling their forecast outputs to grid-scale resource adequacy models. Because these models produce physically consistent, high-resolution trajectories of wind speed, solar irradiance, and temperature simultaneously across the globe, they could replace the fragmented, single-variable statistical forecasts currently used in energy planning, enabling planners to capture cross-variable and cross-regional weather correlations that drive correlated renewable generation shortfalls. This integration could fundamentally shift renewable energy planning from deterministic capacity-factor assumptions to trajectory-ensemble-based risk assessments, reducing the probability of underestimating simultaneous low-wind, low-solar "dunkelflaute" events across interconnected grids.
